references.text: In your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice – the same expression as in 26:5.
God commands Abraham to keep his covenant (mishmarti), which provides context for the phrase 'he kept my statutes' in 26:5.
Moses uses similar terminology: 'keep what he has entrusted to you, his statutes, his judgments and his commandments' – reflecting the words in Gen 26:5.
Blessed are those whose way is blameless, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who keep his testimonies – reflecting Abraham's obedience to God's laws and commands.
By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance, and he went out, not knowing where he was going.
James refers to Abraham's faith and works, including his willingness to offer Isaac, as proof of a living faith demonstrated through obedience.
Complementary perspectives on Abraham's character: obedience (Gen 26) and patient waiting (Heb 6), both leading to God's promise.
Theological dialogue between justification by faith (Rom 4) and the fruit of justification in obedience (Gen 26).
Prophecy (Gen 18) and fulfillment (Gen 26): God's expectation that Abraham would teach his family obedience is confirmed in Abraham's own conduct.
Complementary theology: The faith that justifies (Gal 3) must necessarily be demonstrated in obedience (Gen 26).
Biographical context: The faith that was counted to him as righteousness (Gen 15) resulted in a life marked by obedience (Gen 26).
God's faithfulness (Ps 105) is exercised concretely through Abraham's obedience (Gen 26).
Theological confirmation: James' argument that faith is completed by works (Jas 2) is illustrated concretely by Abraham's obedience in Gen 26.
